idiom_name: withTaskGroup(of:) child tasks (async let for two branches)
implementation_notes: Structured concurrency supplies the fork/join: withTaskGroup spawns a dynamic number of child tasks and the group joins them when the body returns - no child outlives its scope - while async let is the shorthand for exactly two independent branches. The combine is whatever the group body returns; child results must be Sendable to cross isolation boundaries, which is how the runtime enforces the pattern's independence precondition. A task group cannot escape its scope, so the recursion must join inside the function.
pitfalls: A task group is scoped: it cannot be stored or used from a child task, so every branch must be joined inside the body.
Unstructured escapes (Task { }, Task.detached) break the join and may outlive the caller - keep branches as child tasks.
Child tasks cannot touch actor-isolated state; results must be Sendable, so reference-heavy payloads need restructuring before they can be combined.

variants.name: GCD concurrentPerform over chunked ranges
variants.implementation_notes: The pre-concurrency lane: concurrentPerform(iterations:execute:) submits one block to a dispatch queue and runs it across the available cores, returning only when every iteration has finished - the fork and the join in one call. Because it takes an iteration count and not a recursion, a recursive split must first be flattened into chunks, and results are written into index-disjoint slots. Apple's own guidance is to use iterations of at least three times the number of cores so the scheduler can balance; it is the right lane for flat fan-outs over chunks and for runtimes older than Swift 5.5.
variants.code_sketch:
let n = data.count
let chunk = (n + perChunk - 1) / perChunk
DispatchQueue.concurrentPerform(iterations: chunk) { i in      // fork + join
    let lo = i * perChunk, hi = min(lo + perChunk, n)
    results[i] = solve(Array(data[lo..<hi]))                  // disjoint slots
}
let merged = mergeAll(results)                                // combine
pitfalls: Iterations must write to disjoint storage: two iterations touching the same slot is a data race the Swift compiler will not catch here.
concurrentPerform blocks the calling thread until all iterations finish - never call it on the main queue without moving the work off it first.
The iteration count is fixed: the decomposition is flattened before the call, so an uneven workload is not rebalanced below the chunk boundary.
